Let's formulate the theorem exactly:
For a fixed graph H with chromatic number r,
\[
\operatorname{ex}(n,H) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{r-1} + o(1)\right) \binom{n}{2}.
\]
This is the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits theorem.
Alternatively, 
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\operatorname{ex}(n,H)}{\operatorname{ex}(n,K_r)} = 1.
\]
Then with r=3,
\[
\lim = 1 - \frac12 = \frac12.
\]

answer_text:
Let \(P\) denote the Petersen graph, and use the standard (non-induced) extremal number \(\operatorname{ex}(n;P)\).

1. **Chromatic number of the Petersen graph.**  
   The Petersen graph contains a 5-cycle, so it is not bipartite. Hence
   \[
   \chi(P)\ge 3.
   \]
   It is also 3-colorable. For example, in the usual drawing with outer cycle vertices \(v_0,\dots,v_4\) and inner star vertices \(u_0,\dots,u_4\), one may color
   \[
   v_0,v_2:\text{ color }A,\qquad
   v_1,v_3:\text{ color }B,\qquad
   v_4:\text{ color }C,
   \]
   and
   \[
   u_0:\text{ color }B,\qquad
   u_1,u_2:\text{ color }C,\qquad
   u_3,u_4:\text{ color }A.
   \]
   This is a proper 3-coloring. Therefore
   \[
   \chi(P)=3.
   \]

2. **Apply the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits theorem.**  
   For any fixed graph \(H\) with chromatic number \(k\),
   \[
   \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{ex}(n;H)}{\binom{n}{2}}
   =
   1-\frac{1}{k-1}.
   \]
   Taking \(H=P\) and \(k=\chi(P)=3\), we get
   \[
   \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{ex}(n;P)}{\binom{n}{2}}
   =
   1-\frac{1}{2}
   =
   \frac12.
   \]

Equivalently, \(\operatorname{ex}(n;P)\sim n^2/4\), while \(\binom n2\sim n^2/2\).

\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{2}}
\]
